title: Chapter XXXV

teacherSummary.text: Darcy hands Elizabeth a letter explaining himself: he separated Bingley and Jane believing Jane indifferent and the Bennets improper; and Wickham squandered money, demanded more, and tried to elope with Darcy's 15-year-old sister Georgiana for her fortune.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXV develops the idea of the letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of the letter. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXV suggests about the letter. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's point of view and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses point of view in Chapter XXXV to complicate the reader's understanding of the letter. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the letter responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the letter follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior

State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's point of view and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior

Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I had detached Mr. Bingley from your sister” slowly and put it in my own words: Darcy's letter admits that he separated Mr. Bingley from Jane. Next, craft. I notice the precise, legal tone of "detached," as if he were giving evidence in court. The strongest word is “detached”: it is a cold, exact word that admits the act without apology. Then, effect. What does Darcy admit to in his letter to Elizabeth? My answer: Darcy accepts what he did but explains that he believed Jane indifferent; his calm honesty begins to change Elizabeth's view of him.
